questions.question: What is the core philosophy behind React Testing Library?
options: Test components by inspecting their internal state directly
Test components the way a user would interact with them, not implementation details
Only test pure functions, never components
questions.explanation: RTL encourages querying and interacting with the DOM the way a real user (or assistive technology) would, so tests don't break on harmless internal refactors.

questions.question: Why is `userEvent` generally preferred over the lower-level `fireEvent`?
options: It fires a realistic sequence of DOM events (e.g. pointerdown, focus, click) instead of one synthetic event
fireEvent is deprecated and no longer works
questions.explanation: userEvent more closely simulates what actually happens in a browser during a real interaction, catching bugs a single fireEvent call would miss.

questions.question: Why is `getByRole` generally preferred over `getByTestId`?
options: getByTestId doesn't exist in modern RTL
getByRole matches the same way assistive technology does, and failure to query by role often signals missing semantic HTML
questions.explanation: Preferring accessible queries pushes you toward more accessible markup, and avoids tests coupled to arbitrary test-only attributes.

questions.question: In a well-written RTL test for a form component, what should the test generally NOT reference?
options: The visible label text of an input
The component's internal useState variable names
The accessible name of a submit button
The callback prop's arguments after submission
questions.explanation: Testing behavior, not implementation, means the test shouldn't know or care about internal state variables — only what the user can see and do.
